knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5,

  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 150

options(RiskMap.messages = FALSE)

`glgpm()` fits generalised linear models with a spatial Gaussian process in the
linear predictor. As in `glm()`, the `family` gives the distribution of the
response and its link. This article fits each family RiskMap supports, shows
how to name a link or give one as a function, and how exposures and the
parameters of a model are set.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(RiskMap)
library(sf)
```

## Continuous outcomes

A Gaussian model is a linear model with a spatial Gaussian process. The
`italy_sim` data have ten simulated measurements at each of 200 locations in
Italy, and a covariate, the population density. Gaussian models are fitted by
exact maximum likelihood, with no Monte Carlo step.

```{r gaussian}
data(italy_sim)
fit_gaussian <- glgpm(y ~ pop_dens + gp(),
                      data = italy_sim,
                      family = "gaussian")
summary(fit_gaussian)
```

The measurement error variance is the variation of the measurements at a
location around the value of the spatial process there. With several
measurements per location it is estimated well.

## Binomial outcomes and their links

Binomial models need the number of trials, given in `denominator`. The
`liberia` data give the number of people examined for river blindness in each
village and the number found with nodules.

```{r liberia-data}
data(liberia)
liberia <- st_as_sf(liberia,
                    coords = c("long", "lat"),
                    crs = 4326)
liberia <- st_transform(liberia, propose_crs(liberia, messages = FALSE))
```

The string `"binomial"` takes the logit link. A family object names another
link, as in `glm()`. Binomial models take the logit, probit, complementary
log-log and Cauchy links.

```{r binomial-links}
set.seed(2026)
fit_logit <- glgpm(npos ~ log_elevation + gp(),
                   data = liberia,
                   family = "binomial",
                   denominator = ntest)
fit_probit <- glgpm(npos ~ log_elevation + gp(),
                    data = liberia,
                    family = binomial("probit"),
                    denominator = ntest)
rbind(logit = unlist(coef(fit_logit)),
      probit = unlist(coef(fit_probit)))
```

The coefficients are on different scales, but the two models describe much the
same prevalence. The fitted prevalences at the villages agree closely.

```{r compare-links}
cor(fitted(fit_logit), fitted(fit_probit))
```

## Imperfect diagnostic tests

A test with sensitivity $s_e$ and specificity $s_p$ finds a positive with
probability $s_e p + (1 - s_p)(1 - p)$ when the true prevalence is $p$. Any
link that is not named in a family can be given as its inverse in `invlink`, a
function of the linear predictor. The fit below takes the logit of true
prevalence as the linear predictor, for a test with sensitivity 0.95 and
specificity 0.98.

```{r imperfect-test}
set.seed(2026)
fit_test <- glgpm(npos ~ log_elevation + gp(),
                  data = liberia,
                  family = "binomial",
                  denominator = ntest,
                  invlink = function(eta) {
                    0.95 * plogis(eta) + 0.02 * (1 - plogis(eta))
                  })
coef(fit_test)$beta
```

The coefficients now describe true prevalence. `check_fit()` adds a row on the
link, because a link given as a function is not known to make the likelihood
log-concave. Custom links are experimental, and how they are given may change
in a minor release.

## Counts

Poisson models take the log link. The `anopheles` data give the number of
*Anopheles* mosquitoes caught at 116 sites in southern Cameroon. Counts often
vary more than a Poisson distribution allows, and a nugget, `gp(nugget = TRUE)`,
adds an independent effect at each site to take up that extra variation.

```{r poisson}
data(anopheles)
set.seed(2026)
fit_poisson <- glgpm(Total ~ elevation + gp(nugget = TRUE),
                     data = anopheles,
                     family = "poisson")
summary(fit_poisson)
```

The check that needs a look is the spatial scale. At about 2.5 km it is
shorter than the median distance between neighbouring sites, so the data say
little about it. `check_fit()` points to its profile likelihood, or to a mild
penalty that stabilises the spatial variance and scale,
`set_control_mcml(pc_prior = TRUE)`.

For counts collected over different efforts, such as trap nights, the exposure
goes in `denominator`, and the mean count is the exposure times the inverse
link of the linear predictor. An `offset()` term in the formula does the same
for an offset on the scale of the linear predictor.

## Overdispersed counts

`negative_binomial()` gives a negative binomial response with the log link,
whose size $\theta$ sets the extra variation, the variance of a count with mean
$\mu$ being $\mu + \mu^2/\theta$. To show what it recovers, the counts below
are simulated at the `anopheles` sites, with `specify_glgpm()` and
`simulate_glgpm()`, from a negative binomial model with size 2.

```{r simulate-counts}
truth <- specify_glgpm(Total ~ gp(),
                       data = anopheles,
                       family = negative_binomial(),
                       parameters = list(beta = 1.5,
                                         sigma2 = 0.5,
                                         phi = 20,
                                         theta = 2))
counts <- simulated_data(simulate_glgpm(truth,
                                        what = "data",
                                        seed = 1))
```

```{r negative-binomial}
set.seed(2026)
fit_negbin <- glgpm(Total ~ gp(),
                    data = counts,
                    family = negative_binomial())
summary(fit_negbin)
```

The size is estimated with an interval that covers its true value. A Poisson
model of the same counts has no parameter for the extra variation, and puts it
into a spatial process with a very short scale, which `check_fit()` flags.

```{r poisson-on-overdispersed}
set.seed(2026)
fit_counts <- glgpm(Total ~ gp(),
                    data = counts,
                    family = "poisson")
coef(fit_counts)
```

With one count per location a negative binomial model can estimate a nugget or
the size, not both.

## The parameters of a model

Every parameter has one name, used by `coef()`, by `start_pars` and
`fixed_pars` of `glgpm()`, and by `specify_glgpm()`. `glgpm_parameters()` lists
those of a model before it is fitted, with their automatic starting values.

```{r parameters}
glgpm_parameters(npos ~ log_elevation + gp(nugget = TRUE),
                 data = liberia,
                 family = "binomial")
```

`fixed_pars` holds a parameter at a value instead of estimating it. Here the
spatial scale is held at 50 km, and the other parameters are estimated with it.
`start_pars` sets starting values in the same way, and `start_pars = coef(fit)`
starts a fit from the estimates of another.

```{r fixed-scale}
set.seed(2026)
fit_held <- glgpm(npos ~ log_elevation + gp(),
                  data = liberia,
                  family = "binomial",
                  denominator = ntest,
                  fixed_pars = list(phi = 50))
coef(fit_held)
```

## Learn more

Chapter [3](https://www.mbgr.org/03_model-fitting.html) of the book
*Model-based geostatistics for global public health using R* treats linear and
generalised linear geostatistical models, with Gaussian, binomial and Poisson
outcomes.
